title: When the Summer Turns
premise: Jonah Thackeray, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who writes romance novels under a pen name while insisting love is a discipline she can out-train, joins her small town's anonymous winter pen-pal program to research her next book. Through letters she falls for a stranger's honesty — only to discover he is Elias Vane, the developer whose family fortune is buying up the harbor and demolishing the lighthouse cottage where she was raised, and with whom she has traded public insults for years. As the sale deadline looms, Jonah must decide whether the man in the letters or the man at the zoning hearings is the real Elias, and whether her own guarded heart is the corruption she should be fighting. In the end, Jonah publishes the truth of their correspondence as her novel, Elias walks away from the development to restore the lighthouse instead, and they meet at its lamp room — no longer strangers, no longer enemies.
about_author: Zephyrine Underhill spent a decade cataloguing maritime archives on the northern coast before turning to fiction, and her prose still smells faintly of salt and old paper. She writes in a converted fog-signal building and claims she has never once fallen in love on schedule.

chapters.title: The Muscle of the Heart
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Opening on the winter harbor, Jonah finishes her third novel and lectures her writing group that love is trainable, containable — a thesis born from watching her grandfather grieve her grandmother. The town librarian announces an anonymous pen-pal program to fund the failing library. Emotional beat: wry self-protection masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Names in a Hat
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the pen-pal drawing, chaos strikes: the organizer mismatches slips, pairing enemies instead of strangers. Jonah draws Elias Vane — heir to Vane Development, currently petitioning to buy the harborfront including her lighthouse cottage. They publicly refuse; the librarian insists rules are rules. Beat: sparks of open hostility.

chapters.title: First Letter, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Both write grudging, weaponized first letters meant to offend. Instead, stripped of names and faces, each accidentally writes something true — Jonah about grief, Elias about his father's expectations. Each is unsettled by the reply. Beat: the first hairline crack in their armor.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. At the zoning hearing, Jonah testifies fiercely against the harbor purchase, and Elias watches her with new, complicated attention, realizing the letter-writer's tenderness and this woman's fury share one voice. His father pressures him to close the deal by spring. Beat: divided loyalties sharpen.

chapters.title: What the Lighthouse Keeps
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah catalogs the cottage — her grandmother's recipes, her novels' first drafts, the lamp-room key — preparing to lose it. Her found family: the librarian, the retired ferry captain, the bakery sisters, rally around her. Beat: warmth of chosen family against encroaching loss.

chapters.title: Correspondence in Earnest
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The letters deepen into confession: Jonah admits she writes romance because she doesn't believe in it; Elias admits he engineers buildings he'd never live in. Neither guesses the other's identity yet, though Jonah notices a phrase she's heard Elias say aloud. Beat: intimacy outpacing suspicion.

chapters.title: Storm Damage
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A November storm cracks the lighthouse seawall; Elias arrives uninvited with his crew and quietly pays for repairs, telling no one. Jonah finds the invoice and misreads it as a developer's PR move, tearing into him publicly. Beat: misunderstanding hardening just as feeling softens.

chapters.title: The Mirror Chapter
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias confronts his reflection after his father praises his ruthlessness, recognizing that he has become the family's instrument — the corruption theme made personal. He drafts a letter admitting he fears he is unlovable by inheritance. Beat: self-loathing meeting the wish to change.

chapters.title: Bakery Truce
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Forced together judging the library's bake sale, Jonah and Elias call a brittle truce. Working side by side, she glimpses the man from the letters — patient, funny, ashamed of his own name. She shoves the recognition down. Beat: attraction she refuses to name.

chapters.title: Deadline on Paper
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The purchase contract's contingency deadline surfaces: sixty days. Elias stalls his father using procedural delays, buying time he tells himself is for the town, not for Jonah. Meanwhile his anonymous correspondent writes something only Jonah would know. Beat: dread and hope braided together.

chapters.title: The Phrase She Wrote
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Rereading her letters for her novel-in-progress, Jonah matches a sentence to something Elias said at the hearing. She tests him with a planted detail; his next letter takes the bait. She now knows — and says nothing, terrified of what knowing will cost. Beat: secret knowledge as isolation.

chapters.title: Lantern Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town's lantern festival; Jonah and Elias walk the seawall, almost tender, both hiding what they know. A near-kiss breaks off when his phone rings with his father's summons. Beat: longing interrupted by the machinery of power.

chapters.title: Father's Ledger
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias discovers his father's ledger: the development includes plans to raze the lighthouse itself, not just the cottage — a detail withheld even from him. He realizes his signature will erase everything Jonah loves. Beat: horror at complicity.

chapters.title: Confession Withheld
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah decides to reveal herself in a final letter, then falters when the town votes to authorize a legal fight — a fight Elias's money will crush. She chooses the town over the truth, and her letters go cold. Beat: sacrifice mistaken for betrayal.

chapters.title: The Cold Reply
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Receiving her sudden frost, Elias assumes his correspondent learned who he is and recoiled. He signs the purchase agreement in a act of wounded self-destruction, then immediately regrets it. Beat: two people hurting each other with silence.

chapters.title: Revelation at the Library
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The librarian, unable to bear it, reveals both identities at the pen-pal finale reading — reading one of Jonah's own letters aloud to the assembled town, with Elias in the front row. Public exposure, private devastation. Beat: climax of shame and truth.

chapters.title: What You Signed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Jonah confronts Elias about the signed agreement; he confesses the lighthouse clause and his father's manipulation, offering her the one thing he can still do: testimony. She doesn't forgive him — not yet — but takes the documents. Beat: anger transmuting into alliance.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias testifies against his own company before the county board, burning his inheritance and his father's regard in one afternoon. Jonah watches from the gallery, heart training itself toward a new discipline: belief. Beat: power renounced; character proven.

chapters.title: The Lamp Room Key
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The deal collapses; the harbor trust, funded by Elias's redirected settlement, buys the light. Jonah climbs to the lamp room with the old key and finally weeps for her grandparents — and admits her heart was never containable at all. Beat: grief and release.

chapters.title: Last Letter, Signed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Elias leaves one true letter, signed, in the library's return slot — no anonymity left, asking nothing. Jonah reads it standing in the snow, then goes home and writes the ending of her novel with his words woven through it. Beat: vulnerability answered with craft.

chapters.title: When the Summer Turns
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Summer: the relit lighthouse opens as a writers' retreat run by their found family. Jonah gives Elias the manuscript — their story, names intact. On the gallery deck he asks if the heart can really be trained; she says yes, hers took twenty-two chapters. Beat: joy earned, wit restored.

chapters.title: Epilogue: First Light
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. One year later, Elias keeps the lamp's first watch of the season while Jonah sleeps below, her new book dedication visible on the desk: 'For the stranger who was never a stranger.' The harbor glitters; the family he chose waves from the dock. Beat: peace, belonging, dawn.
